### Two sensors, one bath, at the same time {#sec-t1-together}

This experiment calibrates an **NTC thermistor** in a resistive divider and a
**Pt1000** in a bridge with an instrumentation amplifier, in the same bath at
the same instants. That is deliberate: if the two sensors are calibrated
separately, in separate sessions, a difference between their fitted curves
could be the sensors, or it could be that the two baths were not at the same
temperature. Reading them together removes that confound — whatever the
reference thermometer reads at each point is what *both* fits are checked
against, so any difference between the two calibrations is the sensors, and
only the sensors.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### The NTC: Steinhart–Hart {#sec-t1-ntc}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### The NTC: Steinhart–Hart (1)
:::

An NTC thermistor's resistance falls with temperature, steeply and
nonlinearly. The Steinhart–Hart equation is the standard empirical model
[@steinhart1968]:

$$
\frac{1}{T} = A + B\ln R + C(\ln R)^3
$$ {#eq-t1-sh}

with $T$ in kelvin and $R$ the thermistor's resistance. It looks like a
three-parameter nonlinear fit, but it is not: it is **linear in $A$, $B$ and
$C$**, because $\ln R$ and $(\ln R)^3$ are just two more columns of data once
$R$ has been measured.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### The NTC: Steinhart–Hart (2)
:::

Writing $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = \ln R$, $x_3 = (\ln R)^3$ and
$y = 1/T$,

$$
y = A\,x_1 + B\,x_2 + C\,x_3
$$ {#eq-t1-sh-linear}

is an ordinary least-squares problem, solved exactly the way
[S1 fits offset and gain](../S1-daq-static/handbook.qmd#eq-s1-fit) — except
with three columns instead of two. No iteration, no starting guess, no risk of
the fit not converging: the price of the cubic term is one extra column, not
a different kind of problem.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
A simpler, physically motivated special case sets $C = 0$: the **beta
equation**,

$$
R(T) = R_{25}\exp\left[\beta\left(\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{T_{25}}\right)\right]
$$ {#eq-t1-beta}

with $T_{25} = 298.15$ K. This is the two-parameter model most datasheets
quote ($\beta$ is the number on the label), and it is exact only if the true
curve has no cubic term. Fitting the full @eq-t1-sh-linear to real data and
finding $C$ small compared with its own uncertainty is evidence the beta
equation was good enough; finding it *not* small is evidence it was not — and
you cannot tell which, without doing the three-parameter fit.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### The NTC: Steinhart–Hart (3)
:::

The resistance itself is not measured directly. The divider ([@sec-t1-sensitivity]{.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}[@sec-t1-sensitivity-rj]{.content-visible when-format="revealjs"})
gives a voltage, from which $R$ is recovered algebraically; averaging in
**voltage**, at each bath point, and inverting once, is preferable to
inverting every sample and averaging temperatures — the inversion is
nonlinear, and averaging after a nonlinear step is biased in general (the two
only agree exactly for a linear map). [@sec-t1-sensitivity]{.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}[@sec-t1-sensitivity-rj]{.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} returns to why this
matters more at some points of the range than others.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### The Pt1000: Callendar–Van Dusen {#sec-t1-pt1000}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### The Pt1000: Callendar–Van Dusen (1)
:::

A platinum RTD's resistance is far more linear, and far better standardized.
For $t \ge 0\,^\circ$C the IEC 60751 Callendar–Van Dusen relation is
[@iec60751]

$$
R(t) = R_0\left(1 + A t + B t^2\right)
$$ {#eq-t1-cvd}

with $t$ in degrees Celsius and $R_0$ the resistance at $0\,^\circ$C —
nominally $1000\,\Omega$ for a Pt1000, never exactly that on a real part. $A$
and $B$ are standardized coefficients, common to every sensor built to the
IEC 60751 curve; only $R_0$, and a manufacturing spread in $A$ small enough to
be worth checking, differ from one physical part to the next.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### The Pt1000: Callendar–Van Dusen (2)
:::

This experiment **fixes** $A$ and $B$ at the IEC 60751 values and fits $R_0$
(and, as an extension, $A$) from the bath data — not the other way around.
Fixing the standard's own coefficients and fitting only what is specific to
*this* part is both less work and more honest than fitting all three: with
only six bath points, a free three-parameter quadratic has little power to
separate $R_0$, $A$ and $B$ from each other, while the manufacturing spread
this experiment can actually resolve is in $R_0$.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Fitting $R_0$ and $A$ together, with $B$ fixed, still looks nonlinear —
$R_0 A$ is a product of two unknowns — but it is not. Expand @eq-t1-cvd as

$$
R(t) = R_0\underbrace{\left(1 + Bt^2\right)}_{\text{known}} + \underbrace{(R_0 A)}_{\text{unknown}}\,t
$$ {#eq-t1-cvd-linear}

Treating $x_1 = R_0$ and $x_2 = R_0 A$ as the two unknowns, $R(t)$ is linear in
$(x_1, x_2)$ against the two *known* basis functions $(1+Bt^2)$ and $t$ — an
ordinary least-squares fit again, exactly as @eq-t1-sh-linear was. Recover
$R_0 = x_1$ and $A = x_2/x_1$ afterwards. This is the general trick for a
model that is nonlinear in its parameters only through a fixed multiplicative
structure: pick the basis so the unknowns enter linearly, fit that, and
recover the physically named quantities from the fit by division or
substitution.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Sensitivity: divider versus bridge {#sec-t1-sensitivity}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Sensitivity: divider versus bridge (1) {#sec-t1-sensitivity-rj}
:::

The NTC sits in a plain resistive divider, no amplifier:

$$
V = V_{cc}\,\frac{R}{R + R_t}
$$ {#eq-t1-divider}

with $R$ the fixed resistor and $R_t$ the thermistor. Differentiating by the
chain rule, and writing $\alpha = \dfrac{1}{R_t}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}R_t}{\mathrm{d}T}$
for the thermistor's own fractional sensitivity,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}T}
= \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}R_t}\frac{\mathrm{d}R_t}{\mathrm{d}T}
\approx V_{cc}\,\frac{R\,R_t}{(R+R_t)^2}\,\alpha
$$ {#eq-t1-divider-sens}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Sensitivity: divider versus bridge (2)
:::

(the sign of $\alpha$ is negative for an NTC; @eq-t1-divider-sens gives the
magnitude). Two things follow directly from the shape of this expression.
First, $R\,R_t/(R+R_t)^2$ is maximized — for fixed $R_t$ — when $R = R_t$, so
a divider's sensitivity peaks where the fixed resistor matches the
thermistor's *own* resistance, and falls away on both sides of that point.
Second, $\alpha$ itself is far from constant for an NTC: it is large (many
percent per kelvin) near the low end of a typical operating range and smaller
at the high end, because the thermistor's exponential resistance law falls
off in relative terms. A divider sized for good sensitivity at one end of the bath sweep is,
by construction, worse at the other end — a real design trade-off, not a
detail to be corrected after the fact.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Sensitivity: divider versus bridge (3)
:::

The Pt1000 sits in a bridge, read through an instrumentation amplifier of
gain $G$:

$$
V = G\,V_\mathrm{exc}\left(\frac{R_t}{R_t+R_b} - \frac{1}{2}\right) + V_\mathrm{off}
$$ {#eq-t1-bridge}

with $R_b$ the three matched fixed arms and $R_t$ the Pt1000. Differentiating,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}T}
= G\,V_\mathrm{exc}\,\frac{R_b}{(R_t+R_b)^2}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}R_t}{\mathrm{d}T}
$$ {#eq-t1-bridge-sens}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Unlike the NTC, the Pt1000's own $\mathrm{d}R_t/\mathrm{d}T \approx R_0 A$ is
almost constant over the whole industrial range — that is the entire point of
choosing a linear standard curve — so @eq-t1-bridge-sens varies with $T$ only
through the slowly changing $R_b/(R_t+R_b)^2$ term, not through the
sensor's own physics. The bridge's sensitivity is far flatter across the bath
sweep than the divider's, at the cost of needing an amplifier at all.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Sensitivity: divider versus bridge (4)
:::

**The number that matters is not volts per kelvin, it is kelvin per volt of
noise.** [S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd) measured this platform's own ADC
noise floor $\sigma$ directly, on a shorted and a live channel, with no
sensor attached. Dividing that noise floor by @eq-t1-divider-sens or
@eq-t1-bridge-sens, evaluated at an operating point, converts a voltage noise
into a **temperature resolution**:

$$
\delta T_\mathrm{res} = \frac{\sigma}{\left|\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}T\right|}
$$ {#eq-t1-resolution}

This is the honest way to compare two sensor front ends: not by their
sensitivity in V/K in isolation, but by what that sensitivity buys against a
fixed, independently measured noise floor. A front end with high gain and a
noisy amplifier can easily lose to a passive divider read by a quiet ADC — the
comparison in [the analysis tasks](handbook.qmd#sec-t1-tasks) works this out with this experiment's own numbers,
not asserted ones.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Self-heating: an error the excitation creates {#sec-t1-selfheat}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Self-heating: an error the excitation creates (1)
:::

Both sensors are read by passing current through them, and that current
dissipates power in the sensing element itself. The element then sits above
the surrounding medium by [@bentley]

$$
\Delta T_\mathrm{sh} = \frac{P_\mathrm{diss}}{\delta}
$$ {#eq-t1-selfheat}

— the same relation as [the thermal rig's own derivation](../../hardware/thermal-rig.qmd#eq-therm-selfheat)
— with $\delta$ the dissipation constant (mW/K) from the sensor to the bath.
$P_\mathrm{diss}$ for the divider is $I^2 R_t$ with $I = V_{cc}/(R+R_t)$; for
the bridge it is $I_t^2 R_t$ with $I_t = V_\mathrm{exc}/(R_t+R_b)$ the current
through the Pt1000 branch specifically — the other three bridge arms
dissipate power too, but not *in the sensor*, so they do not enter this term.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Self-heating: an error the excitation creates (2)
:::

This experiment measures $\delta$ rather than assuming it, by recording one
extra pair of readings at the *same* bath temperature with a **higher**
excitation on both sensors, and reading the apparent temperature shift through
the already-fitted calibration curve:

$$
\delta = \frac{P_\mathrm{high} - P_\mathrm{low}}{\Delta T_\mathrm{sh,high} - \Delta T_\mathrm{sh,low}}
$$ {#eq-t1-selfheat-fit}

Every quantity on the right is something this experiment already has: the two
powers from the known excitation and the fitted resistance, and the two
apparent temperatures from applying @eq-t1-sh or @eq-t1-cvd to the two
recordings. Because the *low*-excitation reading is also the one every
calibration point uses, $\Delta T_\mathrm{sh,low}$ is close to the baseline the
fitted curve already absorbed, and the interesting number is the extra shift
at high excitation, relative to it.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Self-heating: an error the excitation creates (3)
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Self-heating is why "just increase the excitation" is not free

A bigger excitation gives a bigger signal and, other things equal, a better
resolution in @eq-t1-resolution — but it also dissipates more power in the
sensor, worsening @eq-t1-selfheat. The two trade against each other, and
$\delta$, measured here rather than guessed, is what tells you where the
trade stops being worth it. A well-stirred water bath, with its large thermal
conductance to the sensor, tolerates far more excitation than still air will
in [T2](../T2-temperature-dynamic/index.qmd) — the same $\delta$ that limits
excitation here reappears there as a limit on how fast a sensor can be driven
without lying about the medium it is sitting in.
:::

### An optional third sensor {#sec-t1-thermocouple}

A thermocouple, with cold-junction compensation, would extend this
comparison to a third physical principle (a Seebeck voltage rather than a
resistance) and a genuinely different influence quantity (the reference
junction's own temperature, rather than self-heating). It is not required for
this experiment and no reference data ships for it; a group with time to
spare can build the comparison as an extension, following the sensitivity
and budget structure of [@sec-t1-sensitivity]{.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}[@sec-t1-sensitivity-rj]{.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} and of
[the budget](handbook.qmd#sec-t1-budget) unchanged.
